question: What was our monthly revenue over the last 6 months?
sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC(DATE(oi.created_at), MONTH) AS month, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue, COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders FROM order_items oi WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 6 MONTH)) GROUP BY month ORDER BY month
report: Revenue is computed from order_items.sale_price, excluding cancelled and returned items. Present month over month change in percent and name the best and worst month.
note: Revenue is computed from order_items.sale_price, excluding cancelled and returned items. Present month over month change in percent and name the best and worst month.

question: Who are our top customers by total spend?
sql: SELECT oi.user_id, u.state, u.age, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS total_spend, COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders FROM order_items oi JOIN users u ON u.id = oi.user_id WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') GROUP BY oi.user_id, u.state, u.age ORDER BY total_spend DESC LIMIT 10
report: Customers are identified only by user_id and demographic attributes, never by name or email. Add the share of revenue the top 10 represent.
note: Customers are identified only by user_id and demographic attributes, never by name or email. Add the share of revenue the top 10 represent.

question: Compare the performance of product X and product Y and explain the difference
sql: SELECT p.id, p.name, p.brand, p.category, p.retail_price, COUNT(oi.id) AS units, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue, ROUND(AVG(oi.sale_price), 2) AS avg_price, ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned'), COUNT(oi.id)), 3) AS return_rate FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE p.name IN ('X', 'Y') GROUP BY 1,2,3,4,5
report: Compare units, revenue, average realised price vs retail price (discounting), return rate, and the customer mix (state, age, traffic source) with a second query. Explain the gap with the two or three biggest drivers.

question: Why are users in state X underspending compared to state Y?
sql: SELECT u.state, COUNT(DISTINCT u.id) AS customers, COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS orders, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue, ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(SUM(oi.sale_price), COUNT(DISTINCT u.id)), 2) AS revenue_per_customer, ROUND(AVG(oi.sale_price), 2) AS avg_item_price, ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned'), COUNT(oi.id)), 3) AS return_rate FROM order_items oi JOIN users u ON u.id = oi.user_id WHERE u.state IN ('X', 'Y') GROUP BY u.state
report: Decompose revenue per customer into orders per customer, items per order and price per item; then break down by category and traffic source to find where the gap comes from.

question: Why did our churn rate spike last month?
sql: WITH monthly AS (SELECT user_id, DATE_TRUNC(DATE(created_at), MONTH) AS m FROM orders WHERE status NOT IN ('Cancelled') GROUP BY 1,2) SELECT a.m AS month, COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id) AS active, COUNT(DISTINCT b.user_id) AS retained_next_month, ROUND(1 - SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNT(DISTINCT b.user_id), COUNT(DISTINCT a.user_id)), 3) AS churn FROM monthly a LEFT JOIN monthly b ON a.user_id = b.user_id AND b.m = DATE_ADD(a.m, INTERVAL 1 MONTH) WHERE a.m < DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), MONTH) GROUP BY month ORDER BY month
report: Define churn explicitly (customers active in month M with no order in M+1). Compare the spike month with the previous three, then split by state, category and traffic source to locate the segment driving it.

question: What is the up-to-date revenue by product this year?
sql: SELECT p.id, p.name, p.brand, p.category, COUNT(oi.id) AS units, ROUND(SUM(oi.sale_price), 2) AS revenue FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE oi.status NOT IN ('Cancelled', 'Returned') AND oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR)) GROUP BY p.id, p.name, p.brand, p.category ORDER BY revenue DESC LIMIT 20
report:
# Year-to-date revenue by product

Revenue is the sum of order_items.sale_price for items that are not cancelled or returned, from 1 January to today. The top 20 products are listed with units and revenue; the long tail is summarised as one line. Note that the dataset's orders run into the future, so 'today' must be CURRENT_DATE(), not the max order date.

## Action items
1. Re-stock the top 5 products before the next campaign.
2. Review pricing of products with high units but low revenue.
3. Check return rates of the top 20 separately.
note: Revenue = SUM(order_items.sale_price), exclude status Cancelled/Returned, year to date = created_at >= DATE_TRUNC(CURRENT_DATE(), YEAR). Show top 20, summarise the tail in one line.

question: Which categories have the highest return rate and why?
sql: SELECT p.category, COUNT(oi.id) AS items, COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned') AS returned, ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNTIF(oi.status = 'Returned'), COUNT(oi.id)), 3) AS return_rate, ROUND(AVG(oi.sale_price), 2) AS avg_price FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id WHERE oi.created_at >= TIMESTAMP(DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 12 MONTH)) GROUP BY p.category HAVING items >= 200 ORDER BY return_rate DESC LIMIT 15
report:
# Return rate by category (last 12 months)

Return rate = returned items / all items with any status, per category, with a minimum of 200 items so small categories do not dominate. The analyst then compares the top categories by average price and by department (women vs men) to explain the gap: sizing-sensitive categories (dresses, jeans) return more than accessories.

## Action items
1. Add size guidance on the two categories with the highest return rate.
2. Compare return rate by brand inside those categories.
3. Track the rate monthly to see whether changes work.
note: Return rate = COUNTIF(status='Returned') / COUNT(*) per category over the last 12 months, HAVING at least 200 items. Explain with avg price and department; sizing-sensitive categories return more.

question: What data do we have and what questions can we answer with it?
sql: SELECT 'orders' AS table_name, COUNT(*) AS rows_, MIN(created_at) AS first, MAX(created_at) AS last FROM orders UNION ALL SELECT 'order_items', COUNT(*), MIN(created_at), MAX(created_at) FROM order_items UNION ALL SELECT 'products', COUNT(*), NULL, NULL FROM products UNION ALL SELECT 'users', COUNT(*), MIN(created_at), MAX(created_at) FROM users
report:
# What the data covers

Four tables: orders (one row per order with status and timestamps), order_items (one row per item with sale_price and status), products (catalog with brand, category, department, retail_price, cost) and users (customer demographics: age, gender, state, city, country, traffic_source; no personal identifiers). Together they answer questions about revenue over time, product and brand performance, customer behaviour by segment, returns and cancellations, and acquisition channels. The analyst lists the date range and row counts so the executive knows how current the data is.

## Action items
1. Start with monthly revenue and top products for your brands.
2. Ask 'why' questions by segment (state, category, traffic source).
note: Use get_schema and one UNION ALL count query for date ranges. Describe the four tables in business terms (orders, items with prices, catalog, customer demographics without personal data) and list the kinds of questions they answer.
